summary.text: A three-month-old boy presented with a three-week history of progressively worsening generalized vesiculobullous rash that was initially treated as impetigo. He was otherwise systemically well, with gastroesophageal reflux but no other relevant past medical or family history. Examination showed leathery skin thickening, erythema, vesicles, bullae and erosions with a positive Darier's sign, and no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Serum tryptase was elevated at 30.8 μg/L, abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable and KIT D816V testing was negative. Hematology ruled out systemic mastocytosis, and a skin biopsy showing a dense dermal mast cell infiltrate with strong tryptase and CD117 staining confirmed diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis. A bone marrow biopsy was later deferred as tryptase decreased with omalizumab.

He received multidisciplinary care, family education, epinephrine auto-injectors, betamethasone valerate ointment and off-label rupatadine, then ketotifen and montelukast for ongoing pruritus, flushing and blistering. Eight prednisolone bursts were still required in the first 12 months of life. At 11 months omalizumab 150 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks was started, later escalated to 300 mg with the interval shortened to every 3 weeks.

Pruritus, blistering and flushing improved after 2 doses, and after 1 month of omalizumab systemic corticosteroids, montelukast and ketotifen were discontinued. He remained on omalizumab for over 2 years with improved ongoing control, no adverse events and serum tryptase of 6.2 ug/L; symptoms of pruritus and flushing start to return if a dose is missed, and the discussion reports symptom relapse when a dose was missed.
